questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: Working through the mechanism, which substituent is a strong deactivating meta director in electrophilic aromatic substitution?

options.misconception: methyl is an activating ortho-para director
hydroxyl is a strongly activating ortho-para director

questions.explanation: The nitro group withdraws electrons strongly by both induction and resonance, deactivating the ring and directing incoming electrophiles to the meta position because ortho and para attack places positive charge next to the nitro group.

provenance.author: orgchem2-bank-author
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: Given the transformation, decide: which substituent is activating and ortho-para directing despite being deactivating overall?

options.misconception: nitro is deactivating and meta directing
a carbonyl substituent is meta directing

questions.explanation: Halogens withdraw electron density inductively and deactivate the ring, but donate by resonance, which stabilizes the sigma complex for ortho and para attack, so they are ortho-para directors despite being deactivators.

provenance.author: orgchem2-bank-author
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: A written test asks: why does Friedel-Crafts alkylation fail on a strongly deactivated ring such as nitrobenzene?

options.misconception: the electrophile forms but the ring will not react

options.text: The ring is too electron poor for electrophilic attack

questions.explanation: Friedel-Crafts reactions require an electron-rich enough ring to attack the carbocation-like electrophile; strongly deactivated rings such as nitrobenzene do not react, and aniline also fails because it complexes with the Lewis acid.

provenance.author: orgchem2-bank-author
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: In a review session, what is the active electrophile in aromatic nitration using nitric and sulfuric acids?
questions.explanation: Sulfuric acid protonates nitric acid, which loses water to give the linear nitronium ion, a powerful electrophile that the aromatic ring attacks to form a sigma complex.
questions.hint: Nitronium ion is the nitrating electrophile.

provenance.author: orgchem2-bank-author
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: A chemist observes the following: which Lewis acid is commonly used for Friedel-Crafts acylation with an acid chloride?

options.misconception: sodium chloride is not a Lewis acid catalyst
that is used in other contexts, not standard here

questions.explanation: Aluminum chloride coordinates to the acid chloride, generating an acylium ion electrophile that the aromatic ring attacks; the resulting ketone complexes with the Lewis acid and is released on aqueous workup.
questions.hint: Aluminum chloride generates the acylium ion.

provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: A quiz question asks: what distinguishes aromatic sulfonation from nitration and halogenation?

options.text: Sulfonation does not use an electrophile
Sulfonation is reversible on heating with dilute acid

options.misconception: the sulfo group is meta directing but position depends on existing groups

questions.explanation: Sulfonation is reversible, so it can be used as a temporary blocking group: the sulfonic acid can be removed by heating with dilute acid, unlike nitration or halogenation which are essentially irreversible.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: For the sample reaction, what is the key intermediate in electrophilic aromatic substitution?

options.misconception: a phenyl cation is not formed
the process is cationic, not radical

questions.explanation: Attack of the electrophile gives a cyclohexadienyl cation called the sigma complex or arenium ion, whose positive charge is delocalized over the ring before loss of a proton restores aromaticity.
questions.hint: Arenium ion is the sigma complex.

provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: During a lab exercise, a ring bearing both a methyl group and a nitro group undergoes nitration. Which group mainly controls the position of the new substituent?
questions.explanation: When activating and deactivating groups conflict, the stronger activating group controls orientation, so a methyl group directs the incoming electrophile ortho or para even in the presence of a nitro group.

that is used for halide precipitation

questions.explanation: Iron(III) chloride, often generated in situ from iron and chlorine, polarizes the chlorine molecule to generate a strong electrophile that benzene can attack in electrophilic aromatic substitution.
